content: Several pages on Wikipedia utilize Indic scripts to display native representations of names, places, quotes, and literature. Unicode is the encoding standard used on Wikipedia, and it supports various Indic scripts. However, to view or edit Indic scripts, your operating system must have support for Complex Text Layout (CTL) enabled. Older operating systems that lack support for complex text rendering should not be used to edit Indic scripts. This document provides methods to enable complex text rendering based on your operating system or browser. Many of these methods can also be applied to non-Indic complex scripts, such as Arabic. To check if your system supports complex text rendering, compare how your computer renders specific scripts with the correct rendering shown in provided images. If the rendering matches, your system already supports complex text. However, this does not guarantee that you can edit text in those scripts. To edit such text, you need appropriate text entry software installed on your operating system. For example, the Indic IME toolbar project was developed to facilitate typing in Indian languages in web forms, emails, blogs, and search boxes. This tool converts several Indic fonts to Unicode, enabling popular Indian vernacular websites to render correctly without requiring additional font installations. Windows 95, 98, ME, and NT These operating systems do not have built-in support for Indic scripts. Indic scripts can only be viewed properly in Internet Explorer, provided an appropriate Unicode font is installed. Mozilla Firefox does not support Indic scripts on these systems unless a modified version of the program is used. This limitation is due to a bug in Firefox, which was resolved in Firefox 3 Alpha. However, Firefox 3 does not support Windows 98/ME. No Unicode keyboard driver engines (e.g., Indic IME, Baraha IME) are available for these older systems. Users can use online typing tools or offline text editors specifically designed for this purpose. Windows 2000 Windows 2000 supports Devanagari and Tamil scripts, but complex text support must be manually enabled. To view Indic text: 1. Go to Start > Settings > Control Panel > Regional Options > General. 2. In the Language settings for this system frame, check the box next to Indic. 3. Copy the necessary files from the Windows 2000 CD when prompted. 4. Reboot your computer if required. To input Indic text: 1. Follow the steps above to enable complex text support. 2. Select Input Locale and click Add in the Installed input locales frame. 3. Choose the desired language and keyboard layout. Windows XP and Server 2003 These systems support several Indic scripts, including Bengali, Devanagari, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, Kannada, Malayalam, Tamil, and Telugu. Complex text support must be manually enabled. To view Indic text: 1. Go to Start > Control Panel. 2. In Category View, select Date, Time, Language, and Regional Options, then Regional and Language Options. 3. In the Languages tab, select Install files for complex script and right-to-left languages (including Thai). 4. Allow the OS to install necessary files from the Windows XP CD and reboot if prompted. To input Indic text: 1. Windows XP includes built-in InScript keyboards for most Indian languages. Add them via the Control Panel. 2. In Regional and Language Options, click the Languages tab, then Details. 3. Add a keyboard for your desired language and select the appropriate layout. Windows Vista Windows Vista supports a wide range of Indic scripts, including Bengali, Devanagari, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, Kannada, Malayalam, Oriya, Sinhala, Tamil, Telugu, and Tibetan. Complex text support is automatically enabled. To input Indic text: 1. Like Windows XP, Vista includes built-in InScript keyboards for most Indian languages. Add them via the Control Panel. 2. For phonetic typing, Baraha IME is recommended, while Indic IME is suggested for Remington typing. Mac OS 9 and Earlier The Indian Language Kit, available from Apple at an additional cost, provides support for Devanagari, Gujarati, and Gurmukhi. No third-party Unicode solutions are known, though custom-encoded fonts exist. Viewing Indic text is supported in Safari and most Cocoa applications, which fully support rearrangement and substitution for AAT-based fonts. However, Carbon software like Microsoft Word and Adobe Photoshop generally do not support Indic scripts due to broken or non-existent ATSUI implementations. To input Indic text: 1. Enable specific keyboard layouts in System Preferences under the International panel. 2. Switch between enabled keyboard layouts using the input menu in the upper-right corner of the screen. Linux Distributions Linux distributions like Debian, Fedora, and Gentoo support a wide range of Indic scripts. To view Indic text, ensure you have appropriate Unicode fonts installed. Some web browsers may require enabling Pango rendering for proper Indic text display. For example: In Epiphany, enable Pango rendering via GConf. In Mozilla or Firefox, enable Pango rendering by setting the environment variable `MOZ_ENABLE_PANGO=1`. To input Indic text: 1. Use tools like SCIM (Smart Common Input Method) for unified input method support. 2. For phonetic typing, Baraha IME is recommended, while Indic IME is suggested for Remington typing. Additional Notes The Department of Information Technology, India, provides Unicode Indic fonts for most Indian languages. WAZU JAPAN's Gallery of Unicode Fonts is an excellent resource for all Indic scripts.
